title: What technology is
description: Technology is knowledge put to work on the practical jobs of daily life, from stone tools to light switches.

facts.text: Britannica defines technology as the application of scientific knowledge to the practical aims of human life.
Stone tools from Lomekwi 3 in Kenya, about 3.3 million years old, are the oldest known and predate the genus Homo.
Our species, Homo sapiens, evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago.

title: Inventions that changed daily life
description: A few big inventions, from stone tools and the wheel to printing and the electric light, reshaped everyday life; nearly all of them are very recent.

facts.text: Wheels appear in Mesopotamia by about 3500 BCE, both on carts (a Sumerian pictograph of a wheeled sledge) and as the potter's wheel.
Johannes Gutenberg built Europe's first known mechanized printing press and printed his Bible around 1455, making books far cheaper to produce.
In 1879 Thomas Edison developed a carbon-filament incandescent light bulb.

Squeezing 3.3 million years of tools into 24 hours, Homo sapiens (300,000 years) arrives at about 9:49 p.m., wheels (about 3500 BCE) about 2.5 minutes before midnight, Volta's 1800 battery about 6 seconds before, and Edison's 1879 bulb under 4 seconds before.

title: What energy is
description: Energy is the ability to do work. It is stored (potential) or working (kinetic) and is measured in joules.

facts.text: Scientists define energy as the ability (capacity) to do work.

Energy is potential (stored), such as chemical energy in food and batteries, gravitational energy in raised objects and energy in stretched rubber bands, or kinetic (working): motion, heat, light, sound and electricity.
The joule is the SI unit of energy: the work done by a force of one newton acting over one meter.
One joule is about the energy needed to lift a small apple (about 100 grams) one meter.

title: Energy changes form
description: Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another; in most conversions a lot of it ends up as heat.

facts.text: Energy is neither created nor destroyed; when it is used it changes from one form into another.
Food contains chemical energy, which your body stores and turns into kinetic energy when you move.
At best the human body turns only about a quarter of its food energy into motion; most becomes heat, and most of the time the useful share is far lower.

title: Electric current
description: Current is moving charge, counted in amperes. Electrons already in the wire drift slowly, but the push travels almost at light speed.

facts.text: Electrons carry negative charge and protons positive charge; opposite charges attract and like charges repel.
An electric current is a movement of electric charge; in metal wires the moving charges are electrons.
The charge carriers in a wire are electrons belonging to the wire's own atoms; a battery supplies energy, not charge, and charge is not used up in a circuit.
Electrons in a typical wire drift very slowly, roughly a meter or two per hour (about 10^-4 meters per second).
Closing a switch sends the electrical push through the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so electrons everywhere start moving at once.
One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge per second, about 6.2 billion billion (6.2 x 10^18) electrons per second.

title: Voltage
description: Voltage is the energy given to each coulomb of charge: one volt is one joule per coulomb.

facts.text: Voltage measures the energy given to each unit of charge: one volt is one joule per coulomb (NIST: V = W/A, W = J/s, C = A s).
A common teaching analogy compares a battery to the pump that lifts water to the top of a water-park slide: it gives charge energy to flow around the circuit.
Common household battery cells, such as AA cells, provide about 1.5 volts each.

title: Circuits and switches
description: Current flows only around a closed loop of conductors; a switch opens or closes a gap in that loop.

facts.text: An electric circuit is a path for current made of an energy source (such as a battery), devices that use the current (such as lamps) and connecting wires.
Current flows only around a closed conducting loop from one terminal of the source to the other; a break anywhere in a single loop stops the current everywhere in it.
A switch in the open ("off") position leaves a gap, so there is no closed loop and no current; closing it completes the loop.
Metals such as copper are conductors that carry charge easily; materials like paper and plastic are insulators that stop the flow.

title: Series and parallel circuits
description: In series, devices share one path and fail together; homes are wired in parallel so each device has its own branch.

facts.text: In a series circuit everything is on one path: if one bulb is removed the others go out, and a kitchen wired in series would need every appliance on for the fridge to run.
Home wiring is parallel: each light or appliance is on its own branch with the same voltage across it and draws the current it needs.

title: The incandescent bulb
description: An incandescent bulb makes light by heating a tungsten filament until it glows, wasting most of its energy as heat.

facts.text: Incandescent bulbs waste about 90% of their energy as heat; only about 10% becomes light.
In an incandescent bulb, current heats a thin filament that resists it until the filament is hot enough to glow.
Modern filaments are tungsten, which has the highest melting point of the suitable materials.
The glass bulb holds a vacuum or an inert gas so the filament does not oxidize (burn away).
Scientists around the world worked on the incandescent lamp for about 40 years before Edison, and Joseph Swan in England made a similar carbon-filament lamp in 1878.
Edison's team kept testing filaments and settled on bamboo, giving lamps a lifetime of up to 1,200 hours.

title: The LED
description: An LED makes light directly from a semiconductor junction, with no hot filament, using far less energy.

facts.text: An LED (light-emitting diode) is a semiconductor device with no filament: when current crosses the junction between two semiconductor materials, electrons release energy as light, and the material sets the color.
LEDs use at least 75% less energy than incandescent bulbs and last many times longer.

title: Volta's first battery
description: Galvani's twitching frog legs led Volta to build the voltaic pile in 1800, the first reliable battery.

facts.text: In 1791 Luigi Galvani saw frog leg muscles twitch when touched with two different metals and called it "animal electricity"; Volta argued the current came from the metals and the frog only conducted it.

In 1800 Volta built the voltaic pile, alternating zinc and silver (or copper) discs separated by cloth or paper soaked in salt water: the first reliable battery, giving a continuous current, which vindicated his view against Galvani's.
The volt, the unit of voltage, was named in Volta's honor in 1881.

title: How a battery works
description: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy, sending electrons from anode to cathode through the outside circuit; it dies when its reactants are used up.

facts.text: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy: electrons leave the anode, travel through the outside circuit to the cathode, and ions move through the electrolyte inside to balance them.

A battery stops working when its reacting chemicals are used up; a rechargeable one is restored by driving current through it in reverse, which runs the reaction backward and stores chemical energy again.

title: Electricity makes magnetism
description: An electric current makes a magnetic field, as Ørsted saw in 1820; a coil of wire becomes a switchable electromagnet.

facts.text: During an evening lecture in April 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted saw a magnetic compass needle swing to line up across a current-carrying wire: evidence that electricity and magnetism are linked.
Every magnet has a north and a south pole; opposite poles attract and like poles repel.
An electric current makes a magnetic field; current loops are the most common source of magnetic fields.
An electromagnet is a coil of wire around a magnetic core such as iron; its magnetism can be switched on and off, strengthened or reversed by changing the current.

title: The electric motor
description: A motor spins a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, reversing the current each half turn to keep it going; Faraday built the first in 1821.

facts.text: In a motor, a current-carrying coil between magnetic poles feels a turning force that spins a shaft; brushes and a commutator reverse the coil's current every half turn so it keeps turning the same way.
An electric motor turns electrical energy into mechanical energy (motion).
Electric motors run household devices such as fans, pumps, drills, hair dryers and electric toothbrushes.
In 1821 Michael Faraday built the first electric motor, making a current-carrying wire circle around a magnet in a bath of mercury.

title: Electromagnetic induction
description: A changing magnetic field through a coil induces a current, as Faraday found in 1831.

facts.text: In 1831 Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet inside a coil of wire makes (induces) an electric current in the wire.
Induction needs a changing magnetic field: a steady field through a coil induces nothing, and the faster the field changes, the larger the voltage.

title: The generator
description: A generator is a motor run in reverse: turbines spin a rotor inside coils to turn motion into electricity.

facts.text: A generator is a motor run in reverse: force the coil to turn in the magnetic field and current comes out; the same device can work as either.
A generator converts mechanical energy (motion) into electrical energy.
A power-station generator has fixed wire coils (the stator) around a spinning electromagnet (the rotor); turning the rotor makes current flow in the coils.
Generators are spun by turbines driven by steam, falling water, wind or burning gas; most US and world electricity comes from turbine-driven generators.
Solar photovoltaic cells are the exception: they turn sunlight directly into electricity, with no spinning generator.

title: AC and DC
description: Direct current flows one way; alternating current keeps reversing, 60 cycles a second on the US grid, one cycle per turn of a two-pole generator.

facts.text: Direct current (DC) flows steadily in one direction, as from a battery; alternating current (AC) keeps reversing direction.
US grid AC runs at 60 hertz, 60 complete back-and-forth cycles per second; most grids use 50 or 60.
A two-pole generator must spin at 3,600 revolutions per minute (60 turns a second) to make 60-hertz AC, one cycle per turn.
The grid still runs mainly on AC, but LEDs, computers, solar cells and electric vehicles run on DC.

title: Why AC won
description: AC beat Edison's DC because transformers can raise its voltage for efficient long-distance transmission and lower it for homes.

facts.text: On September 4, 1882, Edison's Pearl Street station in New York began supplying direct current to a district of one-quarter square mile: the forerunner of all central power stations.
Transformers change voltage by induction, so they need a changing current: they work with AC but not with steady DC.
DC could not easily be converted to higher or lower voltages, which made sending it long distances a problem; AC could, using transformers.
Higher voltage makes long-distance transmission more efficient and cheaper, while lower voltage is safer in homes; transformers step between them.
From the late 1880s Edison and Tesla fought the War of the Currents; Edison claimed AC was more dangerous and publicly electrocuted animals to prove it.
Westinghouse won the bid to light the 1893 Chicago World's Fair with Tesla's AC, and on November 16, 1896, Buffalo was lit with AC from Niagara Falls.

title: Watts and kilowatt-hours
description: Power is how fast energy flows: a watt is a joule per second, volts times amps; bills charge for energy in kilowatt-hours.

facts.text: One watt is one joule per second, so a 60-watt bulb uses 60 joules of energy every second it is on.
Volts times amperes gives watts: joules per coulomb times coulombs per second equals joules per second.
A kilowatt-hour is 1,000 watts for one hour (3,600 seconds): 3.6 million joules.
Utilities measure electricity in kilowatt-hours, and household electricity is priced per kilowatt-hour.
